Lumber is wood that has been cut from trees and shaped into usable pieces — like long flat boards, thick beams, or planks — so that people can build things with it.

Think of it this way: a tree in a forest is just a tree. But once that tree is chopped down, stripped of its bark, and cut into flat, straight pieces of a standard size at a sawmill, those pieces are called lumber. It is wood in its "ready to use" form.

Lumber comes in rectangular shapes — long, flat, and straight. You've almost certainly seen it if you've ever walked past a construction site or visited a hardware store. Picture stacks of smooth wooden boards, all cut to similar widths and lengths, neatly piled on top of each other. That is lumber.

The pieces can vary quite a bit in their dimensions:

  • Some are thin and narrow, like the flat boards used in walls or flooring.
  • Some are thick and wide, like the heavy beams used to support a roof or a floor.
  • Some are square in cross-section, like wooden posts.

A tree is cut down in a forest. It is then transported to a facility called a sawmill, where large machines slice the tree trunk into flat pieces. These pieces are then dried (either in the open air or in a special drying oven called a kiln) to remove moisture, because wet wood tends to warp and crack over time. After drying, the pieces are often smoothed and cut to standard sizes. The end result — all those uniformly shaped, dry, workable wooden pieces — is lumber.

Lumber is one of the oldest and most widely used building materials in the world. Its uses are enormous in scope:

Construction is the biggest use. When a house is being built, lumber forms its skeleton — the vertical studs inside the walls, the horizontal joists under the floors, the rafters that hold up the roof. Without lumber, most traditional homes simply could not be built.

Beyond houses, lumber is used to build:

  • Furniture (tables, chairs, shelves, bed frames)
  • Fences and decks
  • Barns and sheds
  • Bridges (especially smaller ones)
  • Floors and staircases
  • Window and door frames
  • Packaging crates and wooden pallets

In short, anywhere you need a strong, natural, workable solid material, lumber is a strong candidate.

Not all lumber is the same. It is broadly divided into two categories based on the kind of tree it comes from:

Hardwood lumber comes from trees that lose their leaves in winter (like oak, maple, walnut, cherry, and teak). Hardwood is generally denser and harder, making it ideal for furniture, flooring, and fine woodworking where looks and durability matter.

Softwood lumber comes from trees that stay green year-round — cone-bearing trees like pine, fir, cedar, and spruce. Despite the name "softwood," many of these are still quite strong. Softwood is cheaper, easier to work with, and grows faster, so it dominates the construction industry. Most of the lumber framing a house is softwood.

Lumber also varies by how it is processed:

  • Rough lumber is wood that has just been cut at the sawmill — it has a slightly rough, uneven surface.
  • Dressed (or surfaced) lumber has been smoothed on one or more sides by a machine called a planer, giving it a clean, flat surface. This is what you typically buy at a store.
  • Green lumber is freshly cut wood that still contains a lot of moisture (it hasn't been dried yet). It is cheaper but will shrink and possibly warp as it dries.
  • Kiln-dried lumber has been dried in a controlled oven, making it more stable and less likely to warp. It is the preferred choice for most serious building work.
How Lumber Is Measured and Sold

Lumber is sold in standardized sizes so that builders can plan and buy what they need. You will often hear lumber described with dimensions like "two-by-four" (written as 2×4). This means the piece is nominally 2 inches thick and 4 inches wide. (In practice, after drying and smoothing, it ends up slightly smaller — a 2×4 is actually about 1.5 inches by 3.5 inches — but the name stays the same. This is just a naming convention in the industry.)

Common sizes include 2×4, 2×6, 2×8, 2×10, 4×4, and so on. The length can vary — often 8 feet, 10 feet, 12 feet, or longer.

There is also a unit of measurement called a board foot, which is used when buying lumber in bulk. One board foot equals the volume of a piece of wood that is 1 inch thick, 12 inches wide, and 12 inches long.

The word "lumber" as described above — wood cut for building — is the standard meaning in American and Canadian English, and this is by far the most common global usage today.

However, in British English, the word "lumber" has a somewhat different traditional meaning as a noun: it refers to old, unwanted, bulky items that are stored somewhere and just get in the way — think of a cluttered attic or storeroom full of forgotten junk. In this British sense, if someone says "the attic is full of lumber," they mean it is full of odds and ends and useless old things, not wood planks. (The British tend to use the word "timber" where Americans say "lumber.")

Because American English dominates global media and commerce, the "wood for building" meaning is the one most people around the world will encounter today.

It helps to know how "lumber" sits alongside similar words:

  • Timber — In British English, timber is the word used for wood prepared for building, essentially what Americans call lumber. In American English, "timber" is more often used to refer to trees standing in a forest, or very large heavy beams. ("Timber!" is also the warning shout when a tree is about to fall.)
  • Wood — A general word for the material itself, in any form. Lumber is a specific, processed form of wood.
  • Plank — A single long, flat, thick board. Planks are a type of lumber.
  • Beam — A large, heavy piece of lumber used as a structural support.
  • Log — A section of a tree trunk that has been cut down but not yet processed into lumber. Logs become lumber after they go through the sawmill.

If you want one clear sentence to anchor the meaning in your mind:

Lumber is wood that has been cut from trees and processed into flat, straight boards and beams, ready to be used in building and construction.

Everything else — the types, the sizes, the uses, the differences between hard and softwood — are just details that build on this simple core idea.
